newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Impact of Telebras ruling seen limited.
newsitem.headline: Impact of Telebras ruling seen limited.

text.p: The short-term impact of a court ruling recognizing subscription receipts of a stranded 1990 Telebras preferred share public offering should remain limited as a final ruling may not come for over a year, traders and analysts said.
"The decision is going to take a long time and when it comes it's going to mean very little," said a trader who requested anonymity.

On Wednesday, a regional federal court backed Telebras' 13.7 billion share subscription, rejecting a government appeal lodged in 1992 to block the issue based on allegations that the share price was undervalued.
The government said it would appeal the decision, a process which could take as long as 18 months.

If this week's ruling is upheld, Telebras will award preferred shares to holders of the subscription receipts at a book value of 6.30 reais, a nearly 93 percent discount on Telebras' 85 real book value, a Bear Sterns & Co. report said.
Although such a scenario was seen undermining the value of existing share earnings by about 4 percent, analysts said the ruling's effect on prices would ultimately be overshadowed by other events.

"In the long-run the effect will be nil because there are other issues such as Telebras's privizatization, which are more decisive to the stock price," said Guilherme Archer, Banco Pactual's research department head.
Another factor that could diminish the impact of a future ruling requiring Telebras to issue the receipts was uncertainty over how receipt holders would go to the market to sell their shares.
If they go to the market all at once, it could erode share prices abruptly, whereas a gradual selloff would have a limited impact on prices, analysts said.

In addition, Telebras watchers said a decision to overturn this week's ruling would not have a lasting effect on the firm's share prices. Such a ruling would require Telebras to repay subscription receipt holders a total of between 60 million and 300 million reais, depending on how the court calculates the reimbursement.
"This will mean nothing to Telebras earnings because part of the total (reimbursement) has already been accounted for in the balance sheet," said one analyst.

Regardless of the future ruling, analysts said the end of the process will be very positive for the company. They said it would allow Telebras to move forward with plans to launch Level 3 ADRs and facilitate restructuring ahead of privatization, slated to begin by late 1998.

Meanwhile, the uncertainty was seen fueling market speculation over the giant telecommunications firm, whose benchmark preferred shares fell 3.75 percent to 79.60 reais between Monday and Wednesday. The shares have soared 76 percent this year.

Secondary market trading of the subscription receipts was suspended Wednesday ahead of the ruling by a Brazilian federal court. Trading resumed on Thursday, with market value of the receipts soaring 66 percent by noon to 38 reais, traders said.
